Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 1:69: Further they said in the Pesikta (DeRav Kahana, siman 24): I accepted Ahab's repentance, but I will not accept yours — for a harsh decree had been issued against him, this being what is written (I Kings 21:17-19), "and the word of the Lord came to Elijah the Tishbite," etc., "go down to meet Ahab," etc., "thus says the Lord: in the place where the dogs licked the blood of Naboth, the dogs shall lick your blood, even yours." "And it came to pass, when Ahab heard, that he tore his garments," etc., "and went softly [at]." What is "went softly"? Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi said, he walked barefoot. What is written there? (ibid. 21:29), "have you seen how Ahab has humbled himself before Me?... I will not bring the evil in his days."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 1:70: I accepted the repentance of the men of Anatot, but I will not accept yours — for a harsh decree had been issued against them, as it is written (Jeremiah 11:22), "thus says the Lord, behold, I will punish them," etc., "and a remnant shall not be left to them" — and yet, since they repented, they merited to be genealogically recorded, as is explained in Ezra [Nehemiah] (Nehemiah 11:32).
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 1:71: I accepted the repentance of the men of Nineveh, but I will not accept yours — for a harsh decree had been issued against them, as it is written (Jonah 3:4-5), "and Jonah began to enter the city," etc., "and the men of Nineveh believed in God" — and it is written, "who knows, God may turn and relent." I accepted the repentance of Jeconiah, but I will not accept yours — for a harsh decree had been issued against him, as it is written (Jeremiah 22:28), "is this man Coniah a despised, shattered vessel?"
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 1:72: In Vayikra Rabbah, the tenth parashah, they said, in these words: Rav Acha and Rabbi Avin bar Binyamin said in the name of Rabbi Abba, great is the power of repentance, for it annuls the decree and annuls the oath. The oath, as it is written (Jeremiah 22:24), "as I live, says the Lord, though Coniah son of Jehoiakim were the signet ring on My right hand." And it annuls the decree: "thus says the Lord, write this man childless" (ibid. 22:30) — and it is written (I Chronicles 3:17), "and the sons of Jeconiah, Assir, his son Shealtiel" — "Assir" [prisoner], for he was imprisoned in confinement; "Shealtiel his son," for from him the kingdom of the House of David was replanted. Rabbi Tanchum bar Yirmeyah said, "Assir" — this is the Holy One, blessed be He, who bound Himself with an oath; "Shealtiel" — that He asked ["sha'al El"] the supernal court concerning His vow. — end of quotation.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 1:73: So too they said in the Zohar (parashat Mishpatim 106a, in the Sabba), on this matter of Jeconiah, that repentance annulled the oath and the decree, in these words: the place where the Master of repentance ascends, even the perfectly righteous cannot stand there; and therefore, once he returned in repentance, the Holy One, blessed be He, surely accepted him immediately. We have learned, there is no matter in the world that stands before repentance, and the Holy One, blessed be He, surely accepts everything — and if he returned in repentance, behold, the way of life is ready to receive him; even though he damaged what he damaged, everything is rectified and everything is restored to its rectification — for even regarding that oath before the Holy One, blessed be He, of whom it is written, "the Lord of hosts has planned it, and who shall annul it" — this is a concealed secret.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 1:74: Further, when the Holy One, blessed be He, swears an oath, He swears only conditional upon [the person] not repenting — for there is no word that stands before repentance, and the Holy One, blessed be He, atones for everything: when they perform complete repentance, the Holy One, blessed be He, accepts it — as it is written, "as I live, says the Lord, though Coniah," etc., and it is written, "write this man childless" — and after he returned in repentance, it is written, "and the sons of Coniah, Assir, his son Shealtiel." From here we learn that repentance breaks several decrees and judgments, and several iron chains, and there is nothing that stands before repentance. Therefore it is written (Isaiah 66:24), "and they shall go out and see the corpses of the men who transgressed against Me" — it does not say "who had transgressed against Me" [past tense] but "who transgress against Me" [ongoing], for they do not wish to return in repentance and be comforted for what they did — but once they are comforted, behold, the Holy One, blessed be He, accepts them.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 1:75: Therefore, a person, even though he has transgressed and caused damage where it was not needed, if he returns before Him, He accepts him and has compassion on him — for the Holy One, blessed be He, is full of mercy toward him and is filled with mercy over all His works, in the manner it is said (Psalms 145:9), "and His mercies are over all His works" — and even upon cattle and birds His mercies extend; if His mercies extend to them, how much more so upon human beings who know and recognize their Master, that His mercies extend to them and rest upon them. Therefore David said (ibid. 119:156), "Your mercies are great, O Lord; give me life according to Your judgments" — if mercies extend to the wicked, how much more so to the righteous! Rather, who needs healing? Those with the ailment. And who are those with the ailment? These are the wicked; they need healing and mercy, and the Holy One, blessed be He, has compassion on them, that they not be forsaken by Him, and He does not depart from them, that they might return to Him. When the Holy One, blessed be He, draws near with the right, He draws near, and when He pushes away with the left, He pushes away — and at the time His right hand draws near while pushing away — from this side He pushes away and from that side He draws near — the Holy One, blessed be He, does not withhold mercy from them. Come and see what is written (Isaiah 57:17), "he went on rebelliously in the way of his heart," and it is written after it, "I have seen his ways, and I will heal him; I will lead him also, and restore comforts to him and to his mourners." "He went on rebelliously" — even though the wicked act as they act, in willfulness, walking in the way of their own heart — they receive warning and do not wish to heed it; at the time they return in repentance and take the good path of repentance, behold, healing is ready to receive them.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 1:76: Now one must examine whether the verse speaks of the living or the dead, for the beginning of the verse is not the same as the end and the end is not the same as the beginning — the beginning of the verse indicates the living, and its end indicates the dead. Rather, the verse says: while a person is in his lifetime, and thus "he went on rebelliously in the way of his heart" — because the evil inclination within him has overpowered him, and therefore he goes on rebelliously and does not wish to return in repentance — the Holy One, blessed be He, sees his ways going badly without benefit; the Holy One, blessed be He, says, I must grasp firmly by his hand — this is what is written, "I have seen his ways, and I will heal him" — for they walk in darkness, I wish to give him healing; "and I will heal him" — the Holy One, blessed be He, brings into his heart the ways of repentance and healing for his soul; "and I will lead him" — as it is said (Exodus 32:34), "go, lead the people" — the Holy One, blessed be He, guides him on a straight path, like one who grasps another's hand and brings him out of darkness.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 1:77: "And restore comforts to him and to his mourners" — it would appear that he is [already] dead; but surely he is dead yet alive — for since he is wicked he is called dead. What is "and restore comforts to him and to his mourners"? Rather, the Holy One, blessed be He, does a kindness for human beings: once one enters his thirteenth year and beyond, He assigns two guardian angels with him. — end of quotation. The rest of his words we have quoted in the Gate of Fear.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 1:78: Although we have elaborated at length in quoting this passage, this is because of its great benefit for repentance — for its words humble the heart, and from it you see how great is the merit of repentance, and how great is the Lord's mercy upon His creatures, to bring the ways of repentance into their hearts and raise them from darkness to light and from death to life. Through this, the penitent is aroused to return out of love — for since the Holy One, blessed be He, out of His love for him, brought repentance into his heart or set before him the ways of repentance, it is then fitting that he love Him and do His will. So too Rabbeinu Bachya, the pious author, wrote in Chovot HaLevavot (Gate of Love, ch. 2), that one of the things that arouses love is when one contemplates God's kindness toward him in bearing patiently with his transgressions and in forgiving him.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 1:79: So too they expounded in the Midrash (Vayikra Rabbah, parashah 10), in these words: "his palate is sweetness" — this is the Holy One, blessed be He; see what He says (Amos 5:4), "for thus says the Lord to the house of Israel, seek Me and live" — and you have an even sweeter palate than this (Ezekiel 33:11), "as I live, says the Lord God, I do not desire the death of the wicked," etc. — and you have something sweeter than this: "and when the wicked turns," etc. Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish said, but only for one who regrets [his wickedness]. How so? Rashbi, peace be upon him, taught: behold, one who was entirely wicked all his days and in the end became entirely righteous — of him it is said, "and the wickedness of the wicked shall not cause him to stumble by it." Rabbi Yochanan said, and not only that, but all the transgressions he committed, the Holy One, blessed be He, counts them for him as merits — this being what is written (Psalms 45:9), "myrrh and aloes and cassia are all your garments" — all the betrayals with which you betrayed Me are like myrrh and aloes, at the time they become "cassia" [ketziyot, related to "katzatz," to cut off, i.e., cut off from their evil], and of them it says, "he shall live." — end of quotation. Without doubt, this matter — that sins are counted as merits — applies to one who returns out of love, as is explained in Tractate Yoma (86b).
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 1:80: Further, among those who repented and were accepted, is Manasseh son of Hezekiah. It says in Pirkei DeRabbi Eliezer (ch. 42): Rabbi Yehoshua says, know the power of repentance — come and see, from Manasseh son of Hezekiah, who committed every abomination in the world and did much evil in the world, and sacrificed to other gods, as it is said (II Chronicles 33:6), "and he made his sons pass through the fire in the Valley of Ben-Hinnom," etc., "he did much evil in the eyes of the Lord, to provoke Him" — and he went out to Jerusalem, releasing doves and sacrificing to the whole host of heaven, and the captains of the armies of Assyria came and seized him with hooks in his head, and brought him down to Babylon, and put him in a copper cauldron over fire, and there he called out to all the other gods he had sacrificed to, and not one of them called to him nor answered him nor saved him. He said, I will call upon the God of my fathers with all my heart; perhaps the Lord will do for me according to all His wonders. And when he called upon the God of his fathers, He was entreated by him and heard his prayer, as it is said (II Chronicles 33:13), "and he prayed to Him, and He was entreated by him." At that moment Manasseh said, there is judgment and there is a Judge.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 1:81: Further in Midrash Rut (5:6), in these words: another interpretation, "come here [gushi halom]" speaks of Manasseh. "Come here" — draw near to the kingdom. "And eat of the bread" — this is the bread of kingship. "And dip your morsel in vinegar" — for he soiled his deeds like vinegar with his evil deeds. "And she sat beside the harvesters" — for his kingdom was captured for a time, as it is written (II Chronicles 33:10-11), "and the Lord spoke to Manasseh and to his people, but they did not listen; and the Lord brought upon them the commanders of the army of the king of Assyria, and they captured Manasseh with hooks." Rabbi Abba bar Kahana said, like the Domenican [imprisonment tradition]; Rabbi Levi bar Chayta said, they made for him a copper cage, kindling fire beneath it, and he would cry out, idol of such-and-such, save me! Idol of such-and-such, save me! When he saw that they did not help him, he said, I recall that my father used to read to me (Deuteronomy 4:30), "when you are in distress and all these things have come upon you... for the Lord your God is a merciful God" — I will cry out to Him: if He answers, good; and if not, then all are the same, all faces are equal. At that moment the ministering angels arose and sealed all the windows above, and said before Him, Master of the universe, would You accept in repentance a man who set up an idol in the Sanctuary itself? He said to them, if I do not accept him in repentance, behold I lock the door before all penitents! What did the Holy One, blessed be He, do? He dug a tunnel for him beneath His Throne of Glory, from a place where no angel has power — this being what is written, "and he prayed to Him, and He was entreated by him, and heard his supplication." Rabbi Levi said, in Arabic they call a tunnel "atirah." — end of quotation.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 1:82: Further they said in the Sifrei (Deuteronomy 3:29): "and we dwelt in the valley opposite Beit Peor" — Moses said to Israel, see what transgression I committed, and how many petitions I made, and I was not forgiven — see the transgression you committed, yet the Holy One, blessed be He, tells you, repent, and I will accept it. Rabbi Yehudah says, this teaches that in several places Israel committed a severe transgression, and the Holy One, blessed be He, said to them, repent, and I will accept it, as it is said (ibid. 4:1), "and now, Israel, listen to the statutes and to the judgments," etc.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 1:83: Further they said in Vayikra Rabbah on "and this is the law of the guilt-offering": thus said the Holy One, blessed be He, to Israel: My children, I am He who said to you, I desire only song and one in whom there is no transgression — I have retracted My words. Even if a person commits several transgressions, one worse than another, and returns in repentance, and lowers himself like the earth, and considers himself as though he were half meritorious and half guilty, with a suspended guilt-offering every day, behold I am with him in mercy, and accept him in repentance, and give him sons, males, engaged in Torah and commandments, and they shall guard the words of Torah in their mouths, as it is said (Isaiah 53:10), "and it pleased the Lord to crush him with sickness; if his soul makes itself a guilt-offering, he shall see seed, he shall prolong his days, and the pleasure of the Lord shall prosper in his hand." — end of quotation.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 1:84: Since the merit of repentance is so great, to atone for what a person has done, as is explained in the preceding passages, it is not fitting that a person be negligent about returning in repentance — for His right hand is stretched out to receive the penitent, and the gate is always open; and whoever does not repent, his punishment is great in the World to Come.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 1:85: Our sages, of blessed memory, gave a fitting parable regarding this matter of repentance in Midrash Kohelet (Midrash Zuta ch. 7), on the verse (Job 11:20), "but the eyes of the wicked shall fail, and refuge shall perish from them." They said: a parable of a band of robbers who rebelled against the king; he seized them and imprisoned them. What did they do? They dug a single tunnel and escaped through it. There was one among them who did not flee; in the morning the king found him and said to him, fool, the tunnel was before you and you did not flee! So too the Holy One, blessed be He, says to the wicked, repentance is before you, yet you do not turn back — this being what is written, "and refuge shall perish from them." — end of quotation.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 1:86: Know that this tunnel our sages, of blessed memory, likened it to in this Midrash is the small opening in the letter heh — as we say in Menachot (29b), why was this world created with a heh? Because it resembles a portico, in that whoever wishes to leave may leave. Why does its leg hang suspended? Because if he returns in repentance, he is brought back in through it. And should one try to bring him back in through that leg [the closed part], the matter would not succeed — as Reish Lakish said, Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish said, what is meant by (Proverbs 3:34), "if it concerns the scorners, He scorns them, but to the humble He gives grace"? If one comes to defile himself, they open the way for him; if one comes to purify himself, they assist him. Why does it have a crown-like protrusion [taga]? The Holy One, blessed be He, says, if he returns, I will bind for him a crown like My own. — end of quotation.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 1:87: It follows that his entry through the narrow supernal opening is so that he be hidden from the possessors of judgment — and so it is explained in the Tikkunim (Tikkun 62, 94b), that through repentance one is hidden from the possessors of judgment, in these words: further (Genesis 3:10), "and I saw that I was naked, and I hid myself" — and by what does a person hide from these judgments so that they have no power over him? Through repentance — this being what is written (Psalms 91:1), "he who dwells in the secret place of the Most High" — this is Imma, who is the "secret of the Most High," from whom this Chochmah [is derived], which is recognized only through her. — end of quotation.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 1:88: So too our sages, of blessed memory, explained in Pesachim (119a), on "and the hands of a man were under their wings" (Ezekiel 1:8): Rav Kahana said in the name of Rabbi Yishmael son of Rabbi Yosi, and the rabbis said in the name of Rabbi Yehudah HaNasi, these are the hands of the Holy One, blessed be He, spread out beneath the wings of the Chayot, in order to receive penitents, [protecting them] from the attribute of judgment. — end of quotation.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 1:89: Having spoken of the exhortations to repentance and its greatness, let us now speak of the nature of repentance:
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 2:1: In explaining the nature of repentance, the pious author of Chovot HaLevavot (Gate of Repentance, ch. 1) explained that the nature of repentance is the restoration of a person to the service of the Creator, blessed be He, after his departure from it and his sinning in it. Departure from the service of the Creator occurs in two ways: either through abandoning what the Creator commanded to do and neglecting it, or through doing what He warned against doing, intending thereby to rebel against his Creator.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 2:2: If his departure from service was of the first kind — abandoning what He commanded — the manner of his repentance is that he hasten and increase, from now on, the performance of commandments, Torah, and the like. And if he transgressed a prohibition, his repentance is that he distance that person to the furthest extreme, until he returns to the line of moderation. The parallel to this is a person whose body has fallen ill from food — either because he refrained from eating what maintains his health, or because he ate what harmed him and ruined his health. For the first category, his remedy is to increase for himself the kinds of food fitting for his nature; and if his illness stems from eating what harmed him, his remedy is to guard himself from that food and to conduct himself in a manner opposite to what disturbed his balance, until he returns to an even state. — end of the summary of his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 2:3: According to the words of the Rashbi, peace be upon him, in the Zohar and the Tikkunim, repentance corresponds to whatever the blemish was — as already explained in the Gate of Fear, that the sinner causes the departure of the Supernal Mother from over the children, or the departure of the lower Mother from over the lower worlds, and everything is in accordance with the magnitude of the blemish, so causing the departure. The intent of the word "teshuvah" [repentance/return] is the return of the grades and their rectification to their original state.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 2:4: The parable is of a water channel flowing from a spring, and that water goes to water several gardens, orchards, fields, and vineyards, and a certain fool comes and diverts the water channel to a garbage dump, an empty place with no benefit — the owner of the spring will be angry at him for two reasons: first, that he ceased watering his good gardens, and second, that he damaged and broke the channel.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 2:5: The parallel is more severe in its punishment than the parable — for the sinner, besides having damaged the channels of the flow from reaching their proper place, directs them to a place that angers the King, the Lord of hosts — namely, that he brings holiness out into impurity, a place that ought to be dry and desolate, and instead he waters and moistens it. This matter is found particularly regarding forbidden sexual relations, and one who goes to a gentile woman, and likewise one who emits seed in vain, and similarly with a blemished tongue — for damaging the covenant of the tongue is more severe than damaging the covenant of the flesh.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 2:6: The manner of repentance is to rectify the broken channels and restore the flow to its place, to each and every place according to where the blemish was. If the blemish is in the Supernal Mother, caused by [rearranging the letters] Ra-Yod-Heh, Ra-Yod-Heh — that is, bringing evil [ra] between the letters yod-heh — repentance will cause the letters yod-heh to be unified and the evil removed, and through this the Mother returns to the children. And if the blemish is in forbidden sexual relations — Ra-Vav-Heh, bringing ra between vav and heh — through which the Mother is exiled from her place and a maidservant inherits her mistress's place — his repentance is to remove that evil from there and unify the vav with the heh.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 2:7: All this is called "teshuvah" [return] — the supernal heh returns [tashuv] over the children, and the heh returns to the yod; and likewise the lower Mother returns over the lower worlds, and the heh returns to unify with the vav. This introduction is briefly alluded to in the Tikkunim, and is found at length in other places in the Zohar, in these words, in Tikkun 63 (94b): it says there, on the verse (Psalms 1:1), "happy is the man who has not walked in the counsel of the wicked" — and explains that "Ashrei" [happy] is Imma — "Asher [Imma] brought you out of the land of Egypt" — surely she is repentance, the healing of all illnesses and afflictions, this being what is written (Lamentations 2:13), "who can heal you?" — and of her it is said (Isaiah 6:10), "and he shall return and be healed for him"; "it shall be healing for your navel" (Proverbs 3:8). Happy is he who returns to his own husband — this is the secret of repentance, that it restores that grade that was distanced from its place, restoring it to its place and bringing it near there. At the time the Shechinah is distanced from her husband, it is said of a person (Deuteronomy 28:66), "and your life shall hang in doubt before you" — "your life" is called this, this being what is written (Genesis 2:7), "and He breathed into his nostrils the breath of life" — at the time He brings her near to her husband. — end of quotation.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 2:8: So too it is explained in the Zohar (parashat Mishpatim, end of p. 106), where it says on the verse (Isaiah 57:18), "and I will restore comforts to him and to his mourners" — that when a person sins, the angels who accompany him withdraw from him and are in mourning over him, and when he returns in repentance, they are comforted. They said, of blessed memory: and now that they have returned with him, surely there is comfort on all sides, and now he lives — surely he lives on all sides, holding fast to the Tree of Life, and since he holds fast to the Tree of Life, surely then he is called a "ba'al teshuvah" [master of repentance/return] — for the Assembly of Israel is also called "teshuvah," and he is her "ba'al" [master/husband] — and the early [sages] said "ba'al teshuvah" literally [i.e., as her husband]. Therefore even the perfectly righteous cannot stand at his level. — end of quotation.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 2:9: Here, in this passage, the matter of two "teshuvot" [repentances] is explicitly stated — for what is explained, that the early sages said "ba'al teshuvah" literally, refers to the supernal repentance [Binah]; and since he is truly "ba'al teshuvah" [her husband], surely he also ascends to the place of the yod, where the secret of life is, which is the place of union — this being "he lives, holding fast on all sides." There is a secret in this that is not this passage's place [to elaborate].
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 2:10: It is explained in the Zohar (parashat Vayikra 15b), the matter of these two "teshuvot," and incidentally the matter of the blemish in them is explained, how great it is, and that repentance must correspond to the blemish, in these words: Rabbi Yosi said, it is written (Leviticus 18:7), "the nakedness of your father and the nakedness of your mother you shall not uncover"; and it is written, "she is your mother, you shall not uncover her nakedness" — she is surely your mother; if her nakedness is uncovered, who must return it? Surely the one who uncovered it, must rectify it — for it is taught, when the evil inclination grows great within a person, it is only through those instances of nakedness [forbidden relations], and all sins are bound up with that nakedness. And it is written, "you shall not uncover" — when he is rectified, he is rectified corresponding to that which was uncovered, and this is called repentance.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 2:11: Rabbi Yitzchak said, all the sins of the world are bound one to another, until the Mother is uncovered among them; and when she is uncovered, all those children are uncovered because of her, as it is written (Deuteronomy 22:6), "do not take the mother with the sons" — and when the world is rectified below, everything is rectified, until the rectification ascends to the Holy Mother to be rectified, and she becomes concealed from what was uncovered; therefore (Psalms 32:1), "happy is he whose transgression is forgiven, whose sin is covered" — and then it is called "teshuvah" — repentance indeed, and then it is called Yom Kippur, as it is written (Leviticus 16:30), "from all your sins before the Lord you shall be purified."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 2:12: Here, Rabbi Yosi explains repentance regarding the lower Mother [Malchut], and Rabbi Yitzchak explains repentance regarding the supernal Mother [Binah], who is called Yom Kippur. But we must understand, both according to this one and according to that one, what is the matter of the uncovering. Perhaps it may be said that her garment is Beriah [the world of Creation], and one who blemishes the Kise [Throne] uncovers her from her garment.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 2:13: So too it is explained in the Zohar (parashat Bereishit 23a): they said, surely now we hear what we had not heard until now — surely the Holy One, blessed be He, created nothing that He does not need, and moreover the Torah of Beriah is the garment of the Shechinah. Had man not been destined to be created, the Shechinah would have been without a covering, like a poor man; therefore, whoever sins is as if he stripped the Shechinah of her garment, and this is Adam's punishment. And whoever fulfills a precept of the Torah is as if he clothes the Shechinah in her garment; and therefore they established, regarding the covering of tzitzit and tefillin (Exodus 22:26), "for it alone is his covering, it is his garment for his skin — in what shall he lie down" in exile? — and this has already been established. — end of quotation. Above this the matter is explained further; and so as not to elaborate, we have not quoted his entire text.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 2:14: So too, the garment of the Supernal Mother is the six extremities, in which she clothes herself, and when there is a blemish in them, she is found uncovered; and repentance is to rectify the lower attributes, in which she is covered, and then it is "teshuvah" that she returns over the children.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 2:15: Further it is explained in the Zohar (parashat Vayikra 16a) that repentance ascends up to Keter, in these words: we have learned, at the time deeds below are fitting and Imma is joyful, the Holy Ancient One is revealed and light returns to Ze'ir Anpin, and then all is joy, all is completeness, all is found in blessings, and mercy is ready, and all the worlds are in joy — this being what is written (Micah 7:19), "He will return, He will have compassion on us, He will subdue our iniquities" — who returns? The Holy Ancient One returns to be revealed in Ze'ir — He returns, returns [yashuv, doubled] to be revealed, what had been hidden at first, and all this is called "teshuvah." Rabbi Yehudah said, all is included, all is [expressed] simply, as it is written (Deuteronomy 13:18), "in order that the Lord may turn from His fierce anger and grant you mercy." — end of quotation.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 2:16: Here it is explicitly said, "who returns? The Holy Ancient One." And according to Rabbi Yehudah, the whole of Atzilut, up above Keter, is all called "teshuvah" — this being "the return of YHVH," that is, the unification of the Name in its letters through the Cause of causes, and through this, "and grant you mercy."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 2:17: Further, there, further on, regarding "and he shall restore the stolen thing that he stole" (Leviticus 5:23), it says: whoever wishes to rectify his deeds in the manner we have said — "and he shall restore" — who restores? Rather, it is like one who rectifies his deeds in order to return the springs of water to their places, to water the plantings — for through his sins he causes them to be withheld from them; and therefore "and he shall restore the stolen thing," as explained. — end of quotation. The intent of the author of the passage is that he found a difficulty: it would have been more fitting for the verse to say "and it shall return the stolen thing" [intransitive], for the word "veheishiv" is in the causative [hifil] form — but this is resolved by what he explained: through the rectification of one's deeds, one causes the supernal blessings that were stolen from their place and source to return to their place. It follows that one performs, above, a renewed action, through the rectification of his deeds.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 2:18: Further, further on, at the end of the page mentioned: happy is the portion of the masters of repentance, and happy is the portion of the righteous, for whose sake the world is sustained — this being what is written (Leviticus 5:23), "and it shall be, when he sins and is guilty," etc. What is written above? "Or has found a lost thing and denied it," etc. — for because of this the Holy One, blessed be He, is removed from all, so to speak the Holy One, blessed be He, is not found in His sustenance, for the Assembly of Israel is separated from her place — this being what is written (Jeremiah 7:28), "faithfulness has perished" — what is "faithfulness"? This is the Assembly of Israel, as in (Psalms 92:3), "and Your faithfulness in the nights." "For what reason has the land perished" (Jeremiah 9:11) — and all is one; and we have already established, "perished" [avdah], not "was destroyed" nor "lost" [in a permanent sense] — in the manner of (Isaiah 57:1), "the righteous perishes" — it does not say "destroyed" or "lost" but "perishes" — this being what is written, "faithfulness has perished"; therefore, "and he shall restore the stolen thing or the lost thing." — end of quotation.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 2:19: The intent of their saying "or has found a lost thing" is that the Shechinah is called a "lost thing" when she loses the supernal blessings because of the blemish of those below — and so too, in this manner, "the righteous perishes," which is explained in the Zohar (parashat Bereishit, end of p. 55) as "he loses all those blessings." And in the Tikkunim, Tikkun 11 (26b), they explained, "perishes" — perishes for the Queen [Matronita], and of her it is said (Isaiah 19:5), "and the river shall be dried up and parched." This means that when the Queen is not in her place, blessings are removed from the Righteous One [Tzaddik/Yesod]. And as for saying, regarding "faithfulness has perished," the meaning is that the attribute called "faithfulness," which indicates the blessings, has perished — up to "for what reason has the land perished," that the attribute of Land [Eretz, i.e., Malchut] has lost the blessings — and it all comes to the same path. And in this manner it is also explained in the Zohar (parashat Va'etchanan 266b).
